## Core Overview
- Primary purpose: Introduce Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) to separate web page content (HTML) from presentation and appearance.
- Fundamental themes: CSS rule syntax, selector types (type, universal, class, ID), combinators, pseudo-classes, pseudo-elements, generic containers (span, div), cascading priority, and stylesheet integration methods (inline, internal, external).

## Key Concepts & Selectors
- CSS Rule Structure: Consists of a selector followed by declaration blocks containing property-value pairs separated by colons and terminated by semicolons (selector {property: value;}).
- Selector Types:
  - Type selector: Targets specific HTML element names (e.g., hr, p, h2).
  - Universal selector (*): Matches every element on the page.
  - Class selector (.class-name): Matches elements sharing a non-unique class attribute value. Can be prefixed with element types (e.g., q.blue) for higher specificity.
  - ID selector (#id-value): Targets a single, unique element on a web page.
- Combinators: Define relationships between selectors:
  - Descendant (space): Matches all descendant elements.
  - Child (>): Matches direct children only.
  - Next sibling (+): Matches the immediate following sibling with the same parent.
- States and Parts:
  - Pseudo-classes (:hover): Define special states using a single colon.
  - Pseudo-elements (::first-letter): Style specific parts of an element using a double colon.
- Generic Containers:
  - span: Used for inline text styling.
  - div: Used as a block-level container.

## Exam Takeaways
- Cascading Priority (Highest to Lowest):
  1. Style attribute (inline CSS)
  2. Style element (internal CSS in head)
  3. External CSS file (.css linked via link element)
  4. User browser settings
  5. Browser default settings
- Syntax Rules: Always use a semicolon after every property-value pair. Separate multiple selectors with commas and spaces.
- Best Practice: External CSS files maximize code maintainability by allowing one stylesheet to format multiple pages. Avoid inline styles (style attribute) as they mix presentation with content.
